lesson.title: Time Complexity: Measuring Work Instead of Seconds
lesson.summary: Time complexity is the specific application of Big-O notation to how the number of basic operations an algorithm performs grows with input size, giving a hardware-independent measure of speed.
lesson.body:
Big-O notation is a general tool for describing growth rates, and time complexity is its most common use: describing how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of the input grows. When someone says an algorithm is O(n^2) without further context, they usually mean its time complexity, how many basic steps it performs, not how many bytes of memory it uses, which is space complexity, covered in the next chapter.

To find an algorithm's time complexity, you count basic operations, comparisons, assignments, arithmetic, and array accesses, as a function of the input size n, then express that count using Big-O. Consider searching for a name in an unsorted list of n names.

def find_name(names, target):
    for name in names:
        if name == target:
            return True
    return False

In the worst case, when the target is last or missing entirely, this performs n comparisons, so its time complexity is O(n). Now compare a function that just checks whether a list is empty.

def is_empty(names):
    return len(names) == 0

In Python, len() on a list is a single fast operation regardless of the list's length, so is_empty runs in O(1) time no matter how many names are in the list.

A useful way to build intuition for time complexity is a doubling thought experiment. Imagine find_name takes about 1 millisecond to search a list of 1,000 names in the worst case. Because it is O(n), doubling the input to 2,000 names should roughly double the time to about 2 milliseconds. If instead a different algorithm took 1 millisecond for 1,000 names but ballooned to 1,000 milliseconds for 2,000 names, that would be a strong sign its time complexity is much worse than linear, closer to O(n^2) or worse, and worth investigating.

It is important to remember that time complexity describes a growth trend, not a stopwatch reading. Two O(n) algorithms can have very different real-world running times: one might do a single comparison per element, another might do five. Big-O hides that difference on purpose, because as n grows large enough, the shape of the curve, flat, straight line, or curve that bends upward, matters far more than the constant multiplier in front of it. An O(n) algorithm will always eventually beat an O(n^2) algorithm as n grows, no matter how much slower its constant factor is.

The rest of this unit works through the specific time complexity classes you will see over and over: O(1), O(n), O(n^2), O(log n), and O(n log n), how to recognize each one from code, and how to count operations carefully enough to derive them yourself.
